column1: # Natural alternatives for communicative moves, plus the connected situations
# that teach them. These remain ordinary sentence items; the mission catalog
# groups them into a response palette without storing an exercise in content.
# Columns: id
column3: english
column6: note

column1: # Leave the id off a new row: the build assigns one and writes it back.

column3: Hello, my name is Luis.

column2: Hola, Luis. Soy Marta. Mucho gusto.
column3: Hello, Luis. I'm Marta. Nice to meet you.
Nice to meet you. How are you?
Very well, thank you. And you?
I'm fine, thank you.
I'm glad. See you later.
See you later, Marta.

column1: # ── Encontrarse con una amiga (guided transfer) ──────────────────────────────

column3: Hi, Luis! How are you today?
Hi, Ana.
All good, thanks. And you?

column2: Estoy genial. Tengo un día muy bueno.
column3: I'm doing great. I'm having a very good day.
That's great! I'm glad.

column2: Bueno, tengo que irme. Hasta pronto.
column3: Well, I have to go. See you soon.
See you soon, Ana.

column1: # ── Un saludo en el trabajo (guided transfer) ────────────────────────────────

column3: Good morning, Luis. How are you?
Good morning, Ms López.

column2: Estoy un poco cansado, pero bien. ¿Y usted?
column3: I'm a little tired, but fine. And you?

column2: Estoy bastante bien, gracias por preguntar.
column3: I'm quite well, thank you for asking.

column2: Me alegro. Buen día y hasta luego.
column3: I'm glad. Have a good day and see you later.
You too, see you later.

column1: # ── Conocer a una vecina (independent transfer) ──────────────────────────────

column2: Hola, soy Elena, la nueva vecina. ¿Cómo estás?
column3: Hi, I'm Elena, the new neighbour. How are you?
Nice to meet you, Elena.

column2: Hoy estoy más o menos. ¿Y tú?
column3: I'm so-so today. And you?

column2: Bien, gracias. Estoy un poco cansada.
column3: Fine, thanks. I'm a little tired.

column2: Tienes que descansar. Nos vemos pronto.
column3: You need to rest. See you soon.
Thanks, see you.

column1: # ── Response palette: natural answers to «¿Cómo estás?» ──────────────────────

column3: I'm doing great.
column6: Very positive and energetic.

column3: Everything's good.
column6: Casual and concise.

column3: Quite well.
column6: Positive, but less emphatic.

column3: So-so.
column6: Neither especially good nor bad.

column3: Not great.
column6: A common concise answer meaning things could be better.

column3: I'm tired.
column6: Feminine speaker form; use cansado for a masculine speaker.

column3: I'm a little tired today.
column6: A gently softened tired answer for a masculine speaker.

column3: I'm a little sad.
column6: An honest, gently softened negative answer.

column3: I'm not doing very well.
column6: A clear negative answer that can invite concern.

column1: # ── Response palette: ordering at a café ─────────────────────────────────────

column3: A black coffee, please.
column6: Short, polite and direct.

column2: Quiero un café con leche, por favor.
column3: I'd like a coffee with milk, please.
column6: A dependable full request with quiero.

column2: Para mí, un té con leche.
column3: For me, a tea with milk.
column6: Natural when ordering as part of a group.

column2: Voy a tomar un zumo de naranja.
column3: I'll have an orange juice.
column6: A common way to make your choice.

column3: A water, please.
column6: A minimal everyday order.

column3: I'd like a coffee without milk.
column6: Useful for removing an ingredient.

column3: A tea, but without sugar.
column6: Adds a simple preference with pero.

column3: For now, just a coffee.
column6: Gently indicates that you may add something later.

column1: # ── Response palette: asking for a destination ───────────────────────────────

column3: Excuse me, where is the pharmacy?
column6: Polite and direct.

column3: Excuse me, where is the station?
column6: Slightly more formal with disculpe.

column3: Where is the town centre, please?
column6: The courtesy comes at the end.

column3: Excuse me, I'm looking for the museum.
column6: States the goal instead of asking a direct question.

column3: Do you know where the bank is?
column6: A softer indirect question.

column3: How do I get to the square?
column6: Asks for the route rather than only the location.

column3: Is the bus stop nearby?
column6: Useful when you already know it is in the area.

column2: Necesito ir al hotel. ¿Por dónde voy?
column3: I need to get to the hotel. Which way do I go?
column6: Explains the destination and asks for a route.

column1: # ── Response palette: saying what you want in a clothes shop ─────────────────

column3: I'm looking for a white shirt.
column6: A straightforward item-and-colour request.

column3: I'd like a blue jacket.
column6: Direct and easy to adapt.

column3: I need some black trousers.
column6: Uses necesito when the item is a need.

column3: I'm looking for a green dress.
column6: A natural ongoing-search expression.

column3: Do you have this shirt in red?
column6: Keeps the item and changes the colour.

column3: Is there a larger size?
column6: Asks for a different fit without repeating the item.

column3: I'm just looking, thank you.
column6: A polite way to decline help.

column2: Busco algo cómodo para el trabajo.
column3: I'm looking for something comfortable for work.
column6: Describes the quality and purpose instead of naming an item.

column1: # ── Response palette: confirming a hotel stay ────────────────────────────────

column3: Yes, I have a reservation.
column6: The simplest confirmation.

column2: Sí, una habitación doble para una noche.
column3: Yes, a double room for one night.
column6: Gives room type and duration together.

column2: Tengo una habitación individual para dos noches.
column3: I have a single room for two nights.
column6: A full stay description without sí.

column2: La reserva está a nombre de López.
column3: The reservation is under the name López.
column6: Gives the name the receptionist needs.

column3: It's for three nights.
column6: A concise answer to a duration question.

column3: There are two of us.
column6: Clarifies the number of guests.

column3: I have a room with breakfast.
column6: Clarifies an included option.

column2: No tengo reserva. ¿Hay una habitación libre?
column3: I don't have a reservation. Is there a room available?
column6: Handles the useful unscripted case of arriving without a booking.

column1: # ── Response palette: reacting to a suggestion ───────────────────────────────

column3: Yes, good idea.
column6: Simple positive acceptance.

column3: Perfect, I feel like it.
column6: Warm and enthusiastic acceptance.

column3: Okay, let's go.
column6: Casual and decisive.

column2: Sí, pero un poco más tarde.
column3: Yes, but a little later.
column6: Accepts while changing one detail.

column3: I'd prefer to go to the park.
column6: Offers an alternative rather than rejecting the plan.

column3: I can't today.
column6: A clear practical refusal.

column3: Sorry, I already have plans.
column6: Declines politely and gives a reason.

column3: Maybe another day.
column6: Keeps the relationship open after declining.

column3: I don't really feel like it.
column6: A softer personal refusal.

column3: What if we go to the cinema?
column6: Responds with a different suggestion.

column1: # ── Response palette: describing a real morning ──────────────────────────────

column2: Normalmente me despierto a las siete.
column3: I normally wake up at seven.
column6: A simple time anchor with a frequency word.

column3: First I take a shower.
column6: Begins a sequence clearly.

column3: Afterwards I get dressed.
column6: Adds the next action.

column3: I have coffee and fruit for breakfast.
column6: Personalises the routine with breakfast.

column2: Por la mañana leo las noticias.
column3: In the morning I read the news.
column6: Adds a habitual activity.

column2: Preparo el desayuno en la cocina.
column3: I make breakfast in the kitchen.
column6: Adds both an action and a place.

column2: A las ocho salgo de casa.
column3: At eight I leave home.
column6: Connects an action to a time.

column3: I go to work by bus.
column6: Adds destination and transport.

column3: On Sundays I get up late.
column6: Contrasts a weekend habit.

column2: Antes de salir, limpio un poco la casa.
column3: Before going out, I clean the house a little.
column6: Uses antes de to connect two events.

column1: # ── Decir en qué trabajas (palette options) ─────────────────────────────────

column3: I am a waiter in a restaurant.
column6: Names the job before the place.

column2: Trabajo en un hospital, con niños.
column3: I work in a hospital, with children.
column6: Adds who you work with.

column2: Estudio y trabajo los fines de semana.
column3: I study and work at weekends.
column6: For someone doing both.

column2: Trabajo en casa, con el ordenador.
column3: I work at home, on the computer.
column6: Says where rather than what.

column2: No trabajo ahora, busco algo nuevo.
column3: I'm not working now, I'm looking for something new.
column6: An honest answer when you are between jobs.

column2: Trabajo en una escuela, cerca de mi casa.
column3: I work in a school, near my house.
column6: Adds how near it is.

column2: Tengo dos trabajos, pero me gusta uno más.
column3: I have two jobs, but I like one more.
column6: Says more than the question asked.

column2: Soy profesora de español para extranjeros.
column3: I am a Spanish teacher for foreigners.
column6: A precise job, feminine speaker.

column1: # ── Decir dónde vives (palette options) ─────────────────────────────────────

column2: Vivo en el centro, en un piso alto.
column3: I live in the centre, in a flat high up.
column6: Says the area and the kind of home.

column2: Vivo con dos amigos en un piso grande.
column3: I live with two friends in a big flat.
column6: Says who you live with.

column2: Vivo en una casa, fuera de la ciudad.
column3: I live in a house, outside the city.
column6: For a home away from the centre.

column2: Vivo solo, en un piso muy pequeño.
column3: I live alone, in a very small flat.
column6: Masculine speaker; sola for a feminine one.

column2: Vivo con mi familia, cerca del río.
column3: I live with my family, near the river.
column6: Adds a landmark instead of a street.

column2: Ahora vivo en Madrid, pero soy de un pueblo.
column3: I live in Madrid now, but I'm from a village.
column6: Separates where you live from where you are from.

column2: Vivo encima de una tienda, en una calle ruidosa.
column3: I live above a shop, on a noisy street.
column6: A detail that says how it feels to live there.

column2: Vivo en el mismo piso desde hace diez años.
column3: I have lived in the same flat for ten years.
column6: Says how long, with desde hace.

column2: Un billete para Barcelona, por favor.
column3: One ticket to Barcelona, please.
column6: Short and direct, with the destination first.

column3: I would like two tickets to Madrid.
column6: Says how many at the same time.

column2: Necesito un billete de ida y vuelta.
column3: I need a return ticket.
column6: Names the fare instead of the destination.

column2: ¿Me da un billete para el próximo tren?
column3: Could you give me a ticket for the next train?
column6: Asks for whatever leaves soonest.

column2: Voy a Sevilla, ¿cuánto es el billete?
column3: I am going to Seville, how much is the ticket?
column6: Puts the price question first.

column2: Un billete de autobús para hoy, por favor.
column3: One bus ticket for today, please.
column6: Says which day it is for.

column2: Somos tres y vamos al aeropuerto.
column3: There are three of us and we are going to the airport.
column6: For a group, without the word billete at all.

column2: Perdón, ¿este billete vale para el metro?
column3: Excuse me, is this ticket valid for the metro?
column6: When you already have one and are unsure.

column1: # ── Pedir una cantidad (palette options) ────────────────────────────────────

column2: Un kilo de patatas, por favor.
column3: A kilo of potatoes, please.
column6: The everyday weight request.

column2: Medio kilo de queso, no más.
column3: Half a kilo of cheese, no more.
column6: Half, with a limit made clear.

column3: Three apples and two bananas.
column6: Counted rather than weighed.

column2: Un poco de fruta para dos días.
column3: A little fruit for two days.
column6: Vague on purpose, and perfectly natural.

column2: Dos botellas de agua, las grandes.
column3: Two bottles of water, the big ones.
column6: Adds which size.

column3: Could you get me a kilo of oranges?
column6: The question form a market stall expects.

column2: Solo una barra de pan, gracias.
column3: Just one loaf of bread, thank you.
column6: Small, with the courtesy at the end.

column2: Quiero lo mismo que la semana pasada.
column3: I want the same as last week.
column6: For a stall you go back to.

column1: # ── Presentar a alguien (palette options) ───────────────────────────────────

column2: Este es mi hermano, se llama Pablo.
column3: This is my brother, his name is Pablo.
column6: Relationship first, then the name.

column2: Ella es mi amiga Lucía, del trabajo.
column3: She is my friend Lucía, from work.
column6: Says where you know them from.

column3: Let me introduce you to my father.
column6: The set phrase for making an introduction.

column2: Son mis abuelos, viven con nosotros.
column3: They are my grandparents, they live with us.
column6: Two people at once, plus a detail.

column2: Es mi vecina, la señora Gómez.
column3: She is my neighbour, Mrs Gómez.
column6: A more formal name for an older person.

column2: Este chico es mi hijo, el pequeño.
column3: This boy is my son, the little one.
column6: Distinguishes one child from another.

column3: She is my girlfriend, we study together.
column6: Says what you share rather than who they are.

column2: No la conoces: es mi tía de México.
column3: You don't know her: she is my aunt from Mexico.
column6: Anticipates that the other person will not know them.
